item.title: In/tension modeling: what gives us the right?
item.description: How to navigate opposing voices and lived tensions.By Julia Beard, Naman Mandhan, & Stacie SheldonAsking the Hardest Question First“What gives us the right to make the interventions and choices we are contemplating on behalf of others?” asks Erika Hall, cofounder of Mule Design. For UX professionals, it’s a question worth sitting with. We’re driven by empathy and a desire to solve problems, yet it’s not common practice for us to question our own authority. How often do we stop to ask the question Erika poses — especially when so much of our job involves putting solutions out into the world? In our effort to do good, we risk unintentionally causing harm. Do we recognize how much power and privilege come with that responsibility?In Part One of In/Tension Modeling as a UX research and strategy tool, we explored the reality that when you solve one problem, other problems are naturally created. We also discussed how, while analyzing data, you will often find perspectives that are in conflict with one another, and how it is vital to amplify all perspectives, not just the loud ones.In this Part Two, we go a step deeper into how In/Tension Modeling can be applied to anticipate, prevent, and respond to potential harms while creating solutions. Throughout the design process, it offers a way to continually check the work against Erika’s question: “What gives us the right?” — ensuring that the drive to solve problems is balanced with care for those most affected by the outcomes.Throughout this article, we share examples of how In/Tension Modeling helped us navigate conflicting perspectives and advocate for the lived experiences of those most affected by the outcomes of a solution. While reading these examples you’ll find moments where we often questioned our own authority on highly polarizing topics. Instead of taking sides, we sought to make space for all the voices and used practical tools to find paths forward that minimize harm. These stories demonstrate that staying with the tension, rather than rushing to resolve it, can lead to more inclusive and resilient outcomes.How In/Tension Modeling Works: A Quick MapThe stories in this article move through three recurring steps. You’ll see each of them in action as you read.Step 1: Surface moments of tensionWhile interacting with research findings, we may encounter opinions or experiences that contradict one another. A common question that arises is how to navigate these conflicting needs and goals, which can feel paralyzing. One effective approach is to juxtapose these perspectives. Doing so allows us to see the full spectrum of needs and goals, leading to better understanding and more informed decision-making. Learn more about this step in Part One of In/Tension Modeling as a UX Research and Strategy Tool.Step 2: Identify opportunities and cultivate solutionsWhere there is tension, there is opportunity. Moments of conflict often reveal pain points, but by reframing those pain points as opportunities, we shift from what is not working to what could work better. This mindset helps us approach problem solving with curiosity instead of frustration, and it keeps conversations constructive.Once opportunities have been identified, brainstorm ways to address them. Each opportunity becomes a prompt for generating solution ideas that balance the needs and values represented in the voices from research.Step 3: Assess solution feasibilityOnce solutions have been brainstormed, take time to consider how each one might affect all parties involved. A helpful way to do this is by exploring the relationships between conflicting points of view and using the Range of Tolerance tool to see where each voice falls. This helps identify whether a proposed solution might unintentionally exclude or disadvantage someone.Involving a diverse group at this stage can surface different perspectives and reduce bias. It is also important to remember that solving one problem can sometimes create another. Revisit the preferences and tolerance ranges of each voice to ensure the solution remains balanced and practical.Repeat step three for all solutions.Central to Step 3 is a tool designed to make that assessment visible across every voice in the room: the Range of Tolerance.The Range of ToleranceRange of Tolerance Tool. The Understanding Group.The strength of the Range of Tolerance lies in its honesty. Full agreement is rare. Rather than seeking solutions everyone loves, it helps identify solutions that people can genuinely accept while intentionally mitigating harm or exclusion. When a voice falls outside the range of tolerance, it signals that a proposed solution may lead to disengagement, resistance, or loss of participation.When testing the viability of solutions, the project team looked for options where all voices fall within either the preference zone or the range of tolerance.Preference zone: The proposed solution is ideal for that group.Range of tolerance zone: While the proposed solution may not be their preferred option, they can live with it and it is unlikely to cause harm.Outside both zones: Anything outside the range of tolerance means they are not willing to consent to that solution.It is difficult to find solutions that place every voice in the preference zone, especially when perspectives are in conflict. But aiming for solutions that keep all voices within the range of tolerance is a practical and powerful goal. It allows us to design with all perspectives in mind, rather than feeling forced to choose one over another; or worse, abandoning the effort to design a solution at all.Responsible design does not pick sides and does not ignore harms. It works through the tension.When Every Voice Tells a Different Story: A Case from the FieldTension isn’t always a bad thing; it can actually bring important truths to the surface. The role of a researcher is not to be a peacekeeper–it is to sit with conflicting insights and find a way forward through them. One project brought this challenge into sharp focus: we were asked to work on one of the most polarizing government programs out there, child support. By design, the program can feel like it creates a winner and a loser. If you are paying support, you may feel you are paying too much or that the money is not being spent as intended. If you are receiving support, you may feel you are not getting nearly enough to meet your family’s needs. Those opposing experiences, both valid, make the program emotionally charged for everyone involved.Even people who have never participated in the Child Support Program often carry assumptions shaped by what they have heard from friends, family, or the media. Phrases such as “deadbeat parent” or “they get so much in child support, they probably don’t even spend it on the kids” seep into everyday conversations and influence how we see the system, often in ways that are oversimplified or unfair.Choosing not to act would still leave children bearing the consequences.For this qualitative research project, our goal was to help child support employees build empathy with families by sharing the stories of people who had lived experience with the program. We also recognized that while navigating child support could be incredibly difficult for participants, the work could be emotionally complex and demanding for staff. Heavy workloads and highly sensitive situations could influence how families experienced the system. We were asked to create a storytelling exhibit to help reconnect staff with the human side of their work. To tell these stories authentically, we first needed to listen.The foundation of this research was one-on-one interviews with families connected to the program. We spoke with people who pay child support, who receive it, and who do both. We sought a diversity of voices which included moms, dads, family members with guardianship, individuals who had left the program, and participants whose involvement ranged from just one year to over thirty.As we conducted interviews, we repeatedly heard perspectives that were in direct tension with one another. In one conversation, a parent who pays child support shared that their monthly payments were so high they were being pushed into debt and struggling to maintain a stable home. In the very next interview, a parent who receives child support described that same payment structure as leaving them without enough money to cover basic needs like food, rent, and childcare. Each parent’s experience was real and valid, shaped by their own circumstances, and each revealed how the system could place families in competing positions. Somewhere in the middle of that tension was a child, depending on both.The conflicting voices we heard during family interviews, Illustration customized from StorysetAs a researcher when someone shares a deeply personal experience, especially one that impacts their entire family, you feel a responsibility to honor that. It is not just about listening; it is about carrying their voice forward in a meaningful way. In this case, that responsibility felt heavy. Every possible solution carried a risk. Solving for one group could unintentionally hurt another. And that harm was real. It could mean one group going into overwhelming debt or the other group not having the support needed to care for their family. Choosing not to act would still leave children bearing the consequences.This led us to consider a framework authored by Designit entitled Do No Harm. The framework challenges practitioners to think about the consequences not only of their actions, but also of their inaction. It encourages us to keep moving forward, even if we make mistakes, as long as we do not become passive.“If the design discipline is to evolve into a safer and more conscientious version of itself, we need to develop approaches from within to be able to effectively forecast, prevent, and respond to harm. A disciplinary culture shift is in order, and the Do No Harm framework provides a way towards achieving it.” — Dr. Pardis Shafafi​, Global Responsible Business Lead of DesignitAfter careful reflection, we recognized that doing nothing (not directly addressing the tensions) carried greater consequences than taking action . We chose to adopt the Do No Harm framework with In/Tension Modeling and committed to amplifying the lived experiences we uncovered. That choice gave us a clear path forward; not the easy path, not the fast path, but the honest, difficult, and necessary one. Through In/Tension Modeling, we didn’t just identify points of tension; we stayed with them, worked through them, and sought to fully understand every perspective.The result was a storytelling exhibit built for program staff, organized around the voices of payers, receivers, and people who had experienced both. It wasn’t designed to declare a winner. It was designed to make the full range of lived experiences impossible to ignore, inviting staff to sit with the people behind the cases rather than the cases alone. The exhibit included reflection questions, guiding principles for engagement, and a call to action for teams ready to do something with what they heard. We built it to last beyond the project. The voices we had been trusted to carry forward were at its heart.That process, staying with the tension long enough to honor every voice, is what In/Tension Modeling made possible. And it wasn’t the last time we’d need it.When Empathy Is Not EnoughEven with a strong foundation in empathy and a commitment to honoring every voice, there are moments when progress stalls. Tensions can become so entrenched — politically, emotionally, or institutionally, that traditional methods of facilitation and consensus-building fall short.In another project with a statewide Child Support Program, we encountered exactly this kind of deeply entrenched disagreement over whether families receiving state assistance should be required to participate in the Program. Despite clear direction and shared intentions, the people involved struggled to move forward. The deeper we went, the more it became evident that no amount of storytelling or surface-level agreement could bridge the divide. We applied In/Tension Modeling not only as a research tool, but as a strategic intervention to help people see one another’s perspectives more clearly, and to begin moving past their entrenched positions.The disagreement surfaced when we were helping to shape a future vision for how services would be delivered. In the first phase, we conducted research to understand how staff across the program perceived the current system, while also gathering experiences from the families being served. This work revealed a deeply divided landscape. Two dominant narratives had taken hold, and neither side seemed willing or able to move toward common ground.On one side, some of these stakeholders expressed a desire to change the experience for families receiving state assistance. They described how participation in the program is mandatory for those on assistance, since the state seeks reimbursement through child support collections. Many believe that families often do not understand this requirement when they apply for assistance, or that they lack a real choice because the financial support is essential. Some participants questioned whether this approach truly benefits families, arguing that it can cause harm by reducing autonomy and dignity without generating significant financial return for the state.At the same time, other stakeholders expressed a different perspective: the program should not change because individuals who use and benefit from the services of the state have an obligation to help repay those costs. For this perspective, required participation was not viewed as punitive but as necessary for fairness, accountability, and in some cases protection. They noted that mandatory engagement with state systems can, in certain situations such as cases of family violence, create opportunities for safety, support, or intervention that might not otherwise occur.We wondered how to get past this argument. The more it was discussed the more entrenched it felt. We decided a starting point should be to model the two sides of the debate:As a third party this was our best effort to represent the two sides and we were as intentional as possible to write each voice without bias, knowing that we could not write each side exactly how a person might want to see it represented.One learning we took from this experience was that, next time, we might invite working groups to participate in creating the models themselves. In our case, we did not have enough time to do so (and it remains to be seen if it would have been beneficial or created a sticking point) but the models as written did produce an immediate response. One person said, “I don’t see my idea on here. There is a loophole where we can avoid forcing them into this program if we wish.” We had never heard that idea before and it became a voice in the middle as well as the beginning of a possible solution for today while the deeper issue is still debated.Facing Our Own Biases in the ProcessWhile modeling opposing voices in the child support project helped move the conversation forward, it also revealed something we hadn’t anticipated, our own blind spots. As researchers and facilitators, we’re trained to center empathy and maintain neutrality, but the charged nature of this work pushed us into uncomfortable territory.When tensions mirrored our own deeply held beliefs, it became painfully clear how hard it is to give fair representation to perspectives we personally disagree with. This wasn’t just about the issues at hand, it was a mirror for our own assumptions, and a test of our integrity in the process.We found that when working as organizational and strategic researchers on issues like child support, the emotions run deep, both within the Child Support Program itself and within us as humans doing the work. Perspectives on poverty, personal autonomy, individual agency, and the role of government collided in ways that brought many tensions to the surface, and we often felt those tensions as sharply as the people we were listening to.At one point, facing a major impasse, we turned to modeling the most common positions emerging from our sessions. Writing one side came naturally — it reflected our own views. But the opposing voice? We struggled. Early drafts framed it as misguided, even harmful. That moment revealed just how easily bias can seep in, even with the best intentions.And yet, that struggle was the work.And yet, that struggle was the work. Wrestling with perspectives we disagreed with forced us to slow down, to listen more carefully, and to understand not just what people believed, but why. It demanded more than empathy — it demanded rigor. We’ve come to believe that this kind of effort should be part of the process itself. Having working groups model both their own and opposing voices, then reflect on that experience, could be transformative. For us, it deepened our respect for every position at the table and gave us a better foundation for moving forward together.Lessons Learned#1 Even when every effort is made to listen and honor each voice, some conflicts are rooted so deeply in belief systems, institutional structures, or moral divides that empathy alone cannot bridge them.#2 Creating neutral models of each perspective helped shift the group from argument to reflection. It gave participants a way to see their own positions more clearly and to recognize the logic in others’ views.#3 Writing from perspectives that differed from our own revealed our blind spots. The exercise forced us to confront how easily personal beliefs can shape research outputs, even unconsciously.#4 The discomfort of disagreement and resistance is not a barrier to progress but a source of information about what truly matters to people. Learning to stay with that discomfort, rather than smoothing it over, can produce deeper understanding and more resilient solutions.Two Truths: Power & Privilege.Two things are true but rarely discussed in UX: our roles carry both power and privilege. That power is not always visible, but it is embedded in our roles and the decisions we make every day. Designing for others means making choices that can either support or constrain their lives. That responsibility requires care, humility, and an awareness of our influence because everything we create has the potential to shape someone’s life for better or worse.“All powers have two sides, the power to create and the power to destroy. We must recognize them both, but invest our gifts on the side of creation.” — Robin Wall Kimmerer, Braiding SweetgrassRobin Wall Kimmerer is a botanist and member of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation whose writing explores reciprocity between humans and the natural world. Her words travel well beyond their original context, and that, too, is worth noticing.On a project with an automotive company, we conducted qualitative research to understand drivers’ behaviors, needs, and perceptions of electric vehicles. We spoke with EV, hybrid, and gas-powered drivers and uncovered a wide range of deeply held, often conflicting attitudes: some saw driving an EV as something they could personally do to contribute to a better environmental future, while others depended on gas-powered vehicles to do their jobs and support their families.To capture these tensions, we plotted perspectives on an “In/Tension” scale. Three distinct voices emerged:It was tempting to connect most with the first voice because it aligned with our own values and lived experiences. But designing only for those who think like us risks reinforcing privilege and overlooking important voices. In/Tension modeling reminds us to ask whether we are designing for people who live like us or for the full range of experiences. It also helps track and map how much each voice can tolerate a given solution, which not only supports more inclusive and sustainable design decisions but also reduces the risk of people abandoning a product or reverting to unhelpful behaviors when a solution pushes beyond what they can accept.The car example, and the earlier example around child support, show why it is often not the behavior itself that should be judged or dismissed. Our job is to dig deeper to understand why people act the way they do. Why is someone behind on child support payments? Why is someone opposed to EVs? Jumping straight into solutions without that understanding can lead to harm.A person’s behavior is often shaped by three things: what they are able to do, the circumstances that give them or limit their chances to do it, and the personal drive they feel to act. These elements of capability, opportunity, and motivation work together to influence behaviors. Assuming any of them can cause us to miss the real issue or design a solution that makes things worse. Yet when we understand them, we can remove barriers and, in some cases, help shift an unhelpful behavior into a constructive one.Following each voice in the EV research revealed these deeper factors. For many EV drivers, the switch aligned with personal values and came with few sacrifices. They drove infrequently, had access to free chargers, and found the change easy. For some gas-powered drivers, however, driving was their livelihood. Charging times meant lost income, and towing for work drained battery life. For them, an EV would threaten their ability to provide for their families.Understanding these motivations brought empathy into the process. It showed that even when lived experiences differ, the values behind them — responsibility, care for others, doing what is right — can be deeply aligned. It also challenged us to ask a harder question: Are we truly bettering society if our solutions only work for those who already share our worldview? If our work deepens divides rather than bridging them, we may be reinforcing the very systems we hope to improve.Lessons Learned#1 Solutions that reflect only our own values and lived experiences risk reinforcing privilege and deepening divides.#2 Whether someone is behind on child support payments or rejects EVs, the behavior alone is not enough to understand the problem. Deep research into people’s circumstances and constraints offers a clearer view of the “why,” fostering empathy and reducing the risk of harmful assumptions.#3 Capability, opportunity, and motivation drive behavior. These three factors work together to influence choices. Assuming them can lead to harmful or ineffective solutions, while understanding them can help remove barriers and encourage constructive change.#4 Mapping how much different perspectives can tolerate a solution allows for more inclusive and sustainable design.#5 Design should connect people across differences rather than reinforcing existing inequalities. The goal is to bridge, not widen, divides.When It’s Easier to Choose, and Better Not ToWhile we as UX professionals play a critical role in confronting power, privilege, and opposing viewpoints in our work, it’s equally important to recognize that we operate within a broader ecosystem — one shaped by human relationships, business objectives, technologies, and cultural norms. For us to effectively practice In/Tension Modeling and ask “What gives us the right?” before “How might we?” we need a culture that supports and protects our ability to create that space.A recent project offers a compelling example, while translating research insights into new product features for a customer onboarding experience on an e-procurement platform. During synthesis, it was discovered that customers had diverging preferences for how they wanted to add users to their accounts. Some customers knew exactly who they wanted to add and preferred assigning roles and permissions to specific individuals (a user-first approach). Others had a clear idea of the roles and permissions needed but not who would fill them (a role-first approach).This insight revealed an opportunity to innovate — to meet the needs of those who wanted to assign roles to specific users immediately, and those who needed the flexibility to define roles that could be assigned later. In other words, it was a chance to design for the middle space where tensions and nuance lived.However, when the author presented these findings to the team, they were asked to “pick a side and recommend it.” Rather than exploring a solution that embraced the tension and expanded the range of tolerance, internal biases and power dynamics took over. The process of translating research into product features shifted — from solving real customer problems across the In/Tension spectrum to prioritizing features that satisfied the preferences of the most powerful stakeholders.This example shows how cultural forces within teams such as a bias toward quick decisions, deference to power, or discomfort with ambiguity, can collapse the very tension that leads to better, more inclusive outcomes. Practicing In/Tension Modeling isn’t just about having the right methods; it’s about fostering a culture that makes space for complexity, dialogue, and dissent. That kind of culture won’t always be in place, but naming what’s missing is a step toward building it. Even when we can’t fully hold the tension, choosing to surface it is still meaningful. A hope would be that every conversation that resists oversimplification helps shift the culture, bit by bit, toward one that can hold more.A Practice, Not a PositionSo, what gives us the right?Erika Hall’s question doesn’t have a clean answer, and we’ve stopped expecting one. What we’ve found instead is that the question itself is the practice. Every time we return to it, before a solution, after a finding, in the middle of a disagreement, it keeps us accountable to the people whose lives our work touches. The right, when it exists at all, isn’t ours to keep. We hold it on their behalf, and the work is to be worthy of that.The work is rarely as simple as deciding who is right and who is wrong. Holding tension does not mean finding the perfect middle ground or choosing which side wins. It means staying curious long enough to understand what different perspectives reveal, particularly when they challenge our own assumptions.Across every project in this article, child support families navigating an impossible system, drivers weighing livelihood against climate, customers whose needs got flattened into a stakeholder preference, what we found was the same: the most important insights lived exactly where the tension was hardest to hold. Not on either side of it. In it.We don’t think that changes. We think that’s the work. And we think the practitioners who are willing to stay there, rather than reach for the cleaner answer, are the ones who will build something worth building.What gives you the right? That question belongs to you now.In/tension modeling: what gives us the right? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Stop blaming the model for slow AI. Using Doherty’s threshold as a guideline.
item.description: Two eras of computing, held to the same 400 millisecond standard.Doherty’s threshold set the rules and has now moved from the answer to the acknowledgment. The fix is a week of front-end work and a definition of done, not cheaper inference.Productivity soars when a computer and its users interact at a pace — under 400 milliseconds — that ensures neither has to wait on the other. Below the threshold, work feels like a conversation; above it, each pause breaks the user’s train of thought and errors climb. — Walter DohertyAsk a product team why their AI feature feels slow and you get a shrug wrapped in a technical explanation.The model takes eight seconds.Inference is expensive.Everyone’s model is slow.Buried in the shrug is an assumption: that the 400 millisecond threshold belongs to green screens and the entire single transactions, and generative AI retired it. It actually rewrote the threshold’s job, and the new job sits entirely on the designer’s side of the request.The reality is that Walter Doherty and Ahrvind Thadani were measuring what happens to a person’s attention when a machine makes them wait, and they attached a dollar value to it.What generative AI changed is the shape of the thing measured. It split one event into two — the acknowledgment and the answer — and the threshold followed the acknowledgment.The stakes changed too, and this is the part worth arguing about.In 1982, a slow response cost throughput. In an AI product it costs supervision. Every AI feature assumes a person is paying close enough attention to catch the model being wrong, and attention is exactly what Doherty’s threshold protects.The acknowledgment budget is a supervision budget. Overspend it and the human in the loop check your product depends on quietly stops happening.What Doherty Actually MeasuredThe 1982 paper, The Economic Value of Rapid Response Time, plotted transactions per hour against system response time, and the shape is not a line.Below roughly 400 milliseconds, productivity climbs faster than the time saved can explain, because something changes in the operator rather than the machine. People stop batching their thinking around the pauses. They hold one thread instead of rebuilding context on every return.That was an economic argument before it was a design one, which is why the number still works in a room full of executives. When system response time dropped, the operator’s own think time dropped with it.The threshold was never a statement about how fast a computer can think. It was a statement about how long a person will hold a thought.Milliseconds Make Millions. Speed matters.It keeps getting re-measured.Deloitte Digital found a 0.1 second speed improvement raised retail conversions 8.4% across 37 brands in Milliseconds Make Millions, 2020. And it runs on the same budget conversation does: across ten languages, Universals and cultural variation in turn-taking in conversation found a median gap between turns of about 100 milliseconds.The threshold has also been rewritten before. Jakob Nielsen restated the same physics for the web as three limits — a tenth of a second feels instant, one second holds the flow of thought, ten seconds is the edge of attention — and those numbers have governed interface work since.Rewriting What The Threshold GovernsIn 1982, request and response were one event, and one clock covered all of it.A generative interaction is two events wearing one costume.The turn, which asks whether the system heard youThe work, which asks whether the answer is any goodJosh Clark and Veronika Kindred call the result an intelligent interface in Say Hello to Sentient Design: a system that composes its response in the moment rather than serving a prepared one.Artificial Analysis. Higher is better. Napster, still bad.Artificial Analysis reports time to first answer token in seconds, and for reasoning models that figure includes the thinking the model does before it says anything at all.Teams read that number, conclude the interaction is seconds-scale, and design accordingly. They are treating a measurement of the model as a measurement of the interface. The interface has its own budget, no dependency on inference, and can echo an input in 50 milliseconds on a bad phone.The model is allowed to take eight seconds to return the answer. The initial time after selecting the send button is not.In enterprise software the mistake compounds, because the person using the tool has a queue.Microsoft’s 2025 telemetry in Breaking down the infinite workday has the average Microsoft 365 user receiving 117 emails and 153 Teams messages a weekday, interrupted every two minutes. Put an AI assist on a list that size and a one-second acknowledgment delay is four minutes of unanswered clicks a day, across 270 moments where the person was already being pulled elsewhere.Consumer chat gets one slow turn and a curious user. Work software multiplies it by the queue.This describes what’s in an interaction from Interaction to Next Paint. There are ways we can mitigate presentation delay.Google’s bar is tighter than Doherty’s and applies squarely to the send button: Interaction to Next Paint treats 200 milliseconds or less, at the 75th percentile of real visits, as good. Your prompt box is already held to it, whatever the model does next.Streaming Is Not An AcknowledgmentStreaming is the pattern every team reaches for, and it earns its reputation. Words arriving at the speed you read them make a long answer feel like a conversation instead of a queue.It solves the wrong problem.Luke Wroblewski was making the case against the gap in front of the first token back in 2013, in Mobile Design Details: Avoid The Spinner. The failure people actually feel happens before that: the press that produces nothing, the input that clears with nothing in its place, the thread that sits empty while a reasoning model spends fifteen seconds deciding how to begin.Streaming turns a wait into reading. It does nothing for the half second when there is nothing to read.The gap also moves without warning. Turn on extended reasoning, route to a larger model, add a retrieval step, and the time before the first token stretches while the interface stays the same. The acknowledgment is the only part that holds still when the routing changes.A second failure hides inside the first. A stream that shows motion while the system is stalled, or a progress line narrating steps it is not taking, buys patience with a claim that turns out to be false.Users forgive slowness. They do not forgive being managed.Two clocks, two owners, two sets of rules.Two Clocks, Two BudgetsHere is the frame I would put in the spec: every AI interaction runs two clocks.Clock oneClock one starts when the user commits — enter, click, tap — and stops when the interface proves it heard. Echo the prompt into the thread. Change the button. Put the skeleton where the answer will land. Target 100 milliseconds, treat 400 as the ceiling. This is front-end work with a hard number attached, and it is where the supervision budget gets spent or saved.Most teams run one clock: the final response. There really should two clocks: acknowledgement and the final response.Clock twoIt starts when the request leaves and stops when the answer is usable, and people will wait here, sometimes for a long time, when the wait buys something. Nobody abandons a four-minute research run that returns a report worth four minutes.Duration is not what breaks the exchange. Silence is: a wait with no receipt, no visible progress, and no sense of what it is purchasing. Speed is not the governing rule on this clock — honesty is.Ben Shneiderman put informative feedback among his eight golden rules in 1985, and the rule survives the rewrite intact: show real state, keep cancel available throughout, and if you commit a change optimistically, as Luke Wroblewski described in Performing Actions Optimistically, have a rollback that tells the truth when the write fails.Most teams instrument clock two, because that is what the model dashboard reports, and leave clock one unowned.That is how a product gets a respectable p95 latency chart and a feature that feels dead on the first tap. Clock two already belongs to the platform or applied AI team, the people with leverage over prompts, routing, and caching. Clock one belongs to whoever builds the surface, and nobody wrote it down as a requirement.Put both numbers in one document with a name on each, and the argument about whose problem the slowness is ends.Latency Debt Shows Up In AgentsA run with four model calls, two tool calls, and a retry inherits the acknowledgment problem at every hop, and the pauses add up to more than any single delay predicts.Take a contract review agent which I have done before:Pull the clausesCompare each against the playbookFlag the gapsDraft the redlinesFour steps, a few seconds each, none alarming alone. Most interfaces show one spinner for the run, so nothing tells the user at step two that the agent grabbed the wrong document version.They find out at the end, in a redline they have to unwind. Wroblewski has been cataloging the fix in Showing the Work of Agents in UI: the run’s steps, visible as they happen, so the person can stop it.Watch what people do and you see the 1982 behavior. They batch: fire off the run, switch to Slack, come back later. The mainframe adaptation, wearing a nicer interface.Users who leave the tab do not come back to review your output. They come back to accept it which is not human in the loop.That is the supervision budget, overspent. A collaborative tool becomes a background job, and the review step you designed becomes a rubber stamp. This is the out-of-the-loop problem arriving through the side door, and latency is what opened it. Nobody decided to trust the model more. The interface made supervision expensive.Latency debt does not stay a performance problem. It redesigns the product, and the surface it demands — notifications, run histories, a way back into a task nobody was supposed to leave — is work you never scoped.The Budget You Already OwnDoherty’s threshold survived the command line, the graphical interface, the web, and mobile. Each transition produced people arguing the old numbers no longer applied, and each time the number outlasted them, because it describes attention rather than hardware.Chat is not the exception. The rewrite splits the response a user waits for from the answer a model produces. Teams holding both numbers ship interfaces that feel fast while running models that are not. Teams holding one wait for inference to get cheaper and call that a roadmap.The 400 millisecond line is still the most useful performance number in design, because it is achievable today, without a single change to the model. It used to protect productivity. Now it protects the person you are counting on to check the model’s work, and that is far more expensive to lose.The model’s latency is a vendor’s problem. The first 400 milliseconds are yours.Action ItemsSplit the budget in the spec. Two numbers beside the visual requirements: acknowledgment under 400 milliseconds, answer unbounded but narrated. One team owns each.Echo the input first, always. The user’s text lands in the thread before any request leaves the client. No inference, no network, no excuse.Replace thinking animations with real state. Searching, reading, drafting, calling a tool. If the interface cannot name the step, that is a missing event, not a copy problem.Measure the first tap in the field. Track acknowledgment latency on real devices and networks, the way you track Interaction to Next Paint, not on the demo laptop.Give every wait an exit, and a reason. Cancel, edit and resend, or start over — and say what the wait is buying. People sit through long waits with a visible payoff and abandon short ones without.Audit the agent run hop by hop. Find the silent step and give it a visible state before you spend a quarter chasing faster inference.Stop blaming the model for slow AI. item.title: Federal pressure may force design education to rethink its identity
item.description: Why an earnings test raises uncomfortable questions about art, professional practice, and the value of a degree.Image source: Adobe StockThe Price of a DegreeThe federal government has decided to ask a question higher education has long avoided. What is a degree worth? Under the U.S. Department of Education’s new earnings-accountability framework, undergraduate programs will be judged partly by whether their graduates earn more than workers whose highest level of education is a high school diploma. Most of the framework takes effect July 1, 2027, and a program that fails the earnings benchmark in two of three consecutive award years can lose access to federal Direct Loans. It is a tidy, if uncomfortable, answer to a question that has never been tidy.Now, the knee-jerk reaction within higher education may be to reject this framework entirely. But there is an economic logic worth acknowledging. Students borrowing heavily for a degree have a legitimate interest in whether it will improve their economic position, and so does the government underwriting those loans. A degree can be intellectually valuable and financially questionable at the same time. Dismissing financial return as an inadequate measure of education does not make it irrelevant. Higher education should be capable of holding both ideas at once without forming a committee to decide which one is permissible.What Markets Cannot MeasureBefore turning to what this could mean for design programs specifically, it is worth acknowledging what ought to be an obvious larger problem with the government using economic outcomes to validate educational value. A philosophy degree is not worthless because an engineer earns more. Love, religion, literature, music, art, and the humanities remain places where human beings wrestle with questions markets and empirical methods are not designed to answer.Science can tell us extraordinary things about how the world works. It cannot, by itself, tell us what makes a life meaningful, what is beautiful, or what we owe one another. David Hume famously identified the problem of moving from statements about what is to what ought to be. Modernity has occasionally made a similar mistake, confusing our growing ability to measure things with our ability to determine what matters.There is also a political dimension that complicates the economic argument. The current administration has challenged parts of higher education it considers ideological. Unfortunately, many programs that deserve scrutiny exist alongside, or within the same academic structures as, genuinely valuable programs in the arts and humanities.It is easy to assign blame along partisan lines, but higher education and its political critics both have responsibilities here. Universities cannot expect public funding to place them beyond public scrutiny, and elected officials should not treat entire fields as suspect because some programs have invited legitimate criticism. Taxpayers have a reasonable interest in knowing what they are supporting and whether institutions can justify that support.The problem is that these different forms of scrutiny can easily become entangled. A program may become vulnerable because its graduates earn less, because its subject matter attracts political criticism, or simply because it belongs to an academic category associated with both. Questions about economic value, ideological influence, and public purpose are not the same questions, even when they converge on the same programs.An argument about financial sustainability is not an argument for discarding fields whose value economic measures cannot fully capture. Asking students to borrow heavily for degrees associated with modest earnings, then using those earnings as evidence that the programs were not worth supporting, conflates whether a field deserves support with how its education should be financed.My own instincts, which are not necessarily common within mainstream academia, complicate where I come down on this question. I am generally skeptical of asking taxpayers to subsidize educational programs at all, particularly when there is no clear agreement about what constitutes public value in the first place. Is it higher earnings, employment, economic growth, civic participation, cultural preservation, intellectual development, or some less measurable contribution to human flourishing?But if we are going to make the case for public support, I am not convinced that producing more programmers, scientists, business executives, or other high earners is necessarily a better investment than preserving disciplines concerned with ethics, history, literature, art, religion, and the humanities. It is worth asking whether the world needs more people following the paths of Musk, Bezos, and Zuckerberg, or those of Camus, O’Keeffe, and C.S. Lewis. The latter contributions are considerably harder to put on an earnings statement, but difficulty measuring something is not evidence that it has no value.The Awkward Case of DesignDesign occupies a less comfortable position in this debate because it is both an academic tradition and a professional field. Design education developed largely within art schools, drawing from typography, illustration, visual composition, and studio practice.Many programs remain there today, and students often arrive believing design is professionalized creativity — art with a client, a deadline, and perhaps slightly better odds of dental insurance. Yet many of those same students eventually work in fields shaped as much by research, technology, psychology, business, and human-computer interaction as by studio art.This disciplinary problem has been visible for some time. Before entering academia, while I was still working professionally as a creative director, I published a 2019 article ominously titled The Death of Graphic Design. I argued that digital marketing, web development, UI, and UX were already absorbing more of the work designers were doing.I ended with a prediction that graphic design might one day become a smaller component of marketing, web development, or UI/UX degrees. Seven years later, that prediction may be getting closer to reality, especially with the rise of AI for visual design tasks. One thing is certain, though. Professional boundaries move faster than academic ones.Current labor data point to the same divergence. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects employment for graphic designers to decline 2 percent between 2025 and 2035, while employment for web and digital interface designers is projected to grow 6 percent. The wage gap is equally striking. In May 2025, the median annual wage for graphic designers was $62,960, compared with $104,000 for web and digital interface designers.Those figures do not tell us whether a particular design program would pass the federal earnings benchmark. The occupational data separate graphic designers from web and digital interface designers, while the federal test evaluates earnings at the program level.A single design program may send graduates into both fields, along with other occupations that fall somewhere between them. The figures therefore cannot predict how any particular program will fare under the federal test. What they do show is that “design” already contains professional destinations moving in substantially different economic directions.Imagine a design program in which three-quarters of graduates enter traditional graphic design while the remaining quarter move into higher-paying UX or interface roles. If all of them are evaluated as graduates of the same program, the earnings of the graphic-design majority could obscure the stronger economic outcomes of those entering UX.The reverse is equally possible. Higher-paid UX graduates could raise the program’s overall earnings, making the economic outcomes of a predominantly graphic-design program appear stronger than those of most of its graduates. The problem is not simply that design might be classified incorrectly. A single classification can combine graduates moving into substantially different professions, making the resulting earnings figure a poor description of either group.UX, interaction, digital product, and interface design make these inherited categories particularly awkward. The Bureau of Labor Statistics describes digital interface work in terms of usability, functionality, navigation, and testing, while Nielsen Norman Group’s UX career research finds practitioners arriving from design, psychology, communication, computer science, and other fields. The problem, therefore, extends beyond where design programs are housed or how their graduates are classified. It raises a more fundamental question about whether design is best understood primarily as an artistic discipline at all.Design Without the PedestalNone of this makes design a science, nor does it remove aesthetics, intuition, taste, or creative judgment. It places them inside constraints that distinguish professional design from artistic expression. A designer may adore a typeface, interaction pattern, color palette, or visual style, but the audience is under no obligation to share the enthusiasm. If users cannot read the text, complete the checkout, understand the information, navigate the interface, or trust the product, the designer’s affection is irrelevant.The obvious objection is that moving design closer to technology, communication, psychology, or business risks stripping away some of the studio traditions that have historically defined design education. Not all of those traditions necessarily need to be preserved, but some remain valuable. Studio education teaches making, critique, visual sensitivity, experimentation, ambiguity, and judgment in ways analytics dashboards and usability reports cannot.A design program rebuilt entirely around market demand could produce technically competent graduates with little visual intelligence, historical awareness, or capacity for formal judgment. The goal should not be to sever design completely from the arts, but to stop treating its artistic foundations as a complete description of the discipline.A stronger model would preserve visual composition, studio critique, craft, and design history while creating clearer pathways into research methods, usability and accessibility, behavioral psychology, analytics, and technology. Shared coursework with computer science, communication, psychology, or business need not turn design into any of those fields. It can acknowledge that contemporary designers increasingly move among them. Design’s unique contribution may be precisely this ability to connect making and judgment with human behavior, communication, and systems.Universities are often structurally bad at this kind of interdisciplinarity. Departmental ownership, budgets, course requirements, and faculty lines reinforce the very boundaries contemporary design crosses. Imagine building a university today without inheriting its departments.Would UX design naturally sit beside painting and sculpture? There is a case for it because visual language, creativity, critique, and making matter. It also has a plausible home somewhere between computer science, psychology, communication, and business. The difficulty of locating design is not necessarily evidence of institutional confusion. It may be evidence that the profession itself has become genuinely interdisciplinary.An Opportunity Hidden in a Bad MetricFor design education, the more interesting question is therefore not whether government will mistakenly classify design as art. It is whether universities will continue treating a degree’s historical home as though it fully describes the professional trajectories available within it. A student can begin in an art-rooted curriculum and leave for UX, interaction, interface, product, or systems-level work without experiencing that transition as a clean disciplinary break. The curriculum should recognize that movement rather than force it into an inherited box.The arts and humanities deserve a defense stronger than salaries. Design deserves an academic structure that preserves what it learned from the studio while acknowledging what the profession has become. The federal earnings test is too crude to answer that question for universities. If it forces them to ask it more seriously, something worthwhile may still emerge.Don’t miss out!
